Former Ethereum Foundation developer Trent Van Epps warns that Ethereum could face a funding crisis within the next 3–9 months 🧐

For years, the Ethereum Foundation has followed a “subtraction” strategy—gradually reducing its influence so the network can thrive independently. However, EF still remains a key pillar of legitimacy through its brand, ties to Vitalik Buterin, developer events, and ecosystem coordination.

💰 The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it. 💵🤩

📰 G7: The Flattery Summit

Seven of the world’s richest democracies walk into a room—and somehow it turns into a talent show for one man.

“The G7 summit has turned into a club of sycophants… leaders shower Donald Trump with compliments and gifts… while tolerating his numerous insults,” Frankfurter Rundschau writes.

Diplomacy, 2026 edition: bring your best gift, your softest tone, and your lowest expectations.

The same leaders who sell voters the myth of “strategic autonomy” suddenly look like middle managers trying to survive a volatile CEO. Smile through the insults. Nod through the contradictions. Pretend the agenda still matters.

Sanctions on Russia get recycled like corporate talking points—strong language, minimal risk, maximum optics. Meanwhile, the self-styled “dealmaker” who once promised to end the Ukraine war gets a polite pass. No reminders. No pressure. Just careful choreography.

For Berlin, the optics sting. A country that markets itself as Europe’s backbone now appears as part of a traveling roadshow of reassurance, hoping the U.S. stays predictable for at least one news cycle. Sovereignty, apparently, now comes with a gift receipt.

But let’s not pretend this is new. G7 has always been less a council of equals and more a hierarchy with better catering. Trump didn’t invent the dynamic—he just removed the polite filter.

So what is this summit really? A strategy session—or a live demonstration of how power reorganizes the room without asking permission?

🚨 Top 5 Most Toxic Fabrics (and Why) 

Not all fabrics are safe for you—or the planet. Here’s the science behind the worst offenders:

1️⃣ Polyester: Made from petroleum and treated with antimony (a carcinogen). It also sheds microplastics, harming marine life and potentially entering our food chain.
2️⃣ Nylon: Produced with harsh chemicals like formaldehyde and emits nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas 300x worse than CO₂.
3️⃣ Spandex (Elastane): Made with polyurethane, it’s loaded with toxic solvents that are harmful during production and can cause skin irritation + further issues
4️⃣ Acrylic: Contains acrylonitrile, a carcinogen linked to respiratory issues, dizziness, and headaches.
5️⃣ Bamboo (Non-Organic): Often marketed as “eco-friendly,” but most bamboo fabric is processed with toxic chemicals like carbon disulfide to create bamboo viscose, harming workers and ecosystems.

 The Fix: Choose organic cotton, Tencel (Lyocell), hemp, linen, or wool for safer, more sustainable choices. 🌿

Yours, Steve Johnson
